claim: The study generated 1.89 billion RNA-seq reads from 63 individually recognized adult baboons in the Amboseli population.
source: We obtained blood samples from 63 individually recognized adult baboons in the Amboseli population (Figure 1—figure supplement 1). From these samples, we produced a total of 1.89 billion RNA-seq reads (mean of 30.0 ± 4.5 s.d. million reads per individual, with 8.6 ± 1.8 s.d. million reads uniquely mapped to exons: Supplementary file 1A).
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number of RNA-seq reads generated and the sample size.

claim: On average, 67.2% of reads mapped to the baboon genome (Panu2.0), with 69.2% of mapped reads assigned to a unique location.
source: On average, 67.2% of reads mapped to the most recent release of the baboon genome (Panu2.0), 69.2% of which could be assigned to a unique location.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific percentages of read mapping from the RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: eQTL were identified for 1787 genes (17.2% of analyzed genes) at a 10% false discovery rate.
source: At a 10% false discovery rate, we identified eQTL for 1787 (17.2%) of the genes we analyzed, and evidence for ASE for 510 (23.4%) of tested genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number and percentage of genes with detected eQTL.

claim: Evidence for allele-specific expression (ASE) was detected for 510 genes (23.4% of tested genes) at a 10% false discovery rate.
source: At a 10% false discovery rate, we identified eQTL for 1787 (17.2%) of the genes we analyzed, and evidence for ASE for 510 (23.4%) of tested genes.
evidence: The manuscript directly reports the number and percentage of genes with detected ASE.

claim: eQTL were strongly enriched near gene transcription start sites and in gene bodies.
source: Consistent with reports in humans (e.g., Veyrieras et al., 2008; Pickrell et al., 2010a), eQTL were strongly enriched near gene transcription start sites and in gene bodies (Figure 1; controlling for the background distribution of sites tested, which were also enriched in and around genes).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment patterns and references Figure 1 showing spatial distribution of eQTL.

claim: Genes with eQTL were more likely to exhibit significant ASE and vice-versa (hypergeometric test: p < 10−25).
source: Also as expected, genes with eQTL were more likely to exhibit significant ASE and vice-versa (hypergeometric test: p < 10−25; Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test result showing correlation between eQTL and ASE detection.

claim: The magnitude and direction of ASE and eQTL were significantly correlated when an eQTL SNP could also be assessed for ASE (n = 123 genes; r = 0.719, p < 10−20).
source: The magnitude and direction of ASE and eQTL were significantly correlated when an eQTL SNP could also be assessed for ASE (n = 123 genes; r = 0.719, p < 10−20, Figure 1—figure supplement 7)
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation statistics between ASE and eQTL effect sizes.

claim: Detection of ASE was most strongly favored for highly expressed genes (Wilcoxon test: p < 10−208).
source: Detection of ASE was most strongly favored for highly expressed genes (i.e., higher RPKM: Wilcoxon test: p < 10−208; Figure 1—figure supplement 8)
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test showing relationship between gene expression level and ASE detection.

claim: Detection of eQTL was most strongly favored for genes with high local SNP density (p < 10−72).
source: whereas detection of eQTL was most strongly favored for genes with high local SNP density (p < 10−72; Figure 1—figure supplement 8)
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test showing relationship between SNP density and eQTL detection.

claim: Using the same RNA-seq-based pipeline, 290 genes with eQTL were identified in the YRI data set, representing 41.4% of those identified using independently collected genotype data.
source: Indeed, when eQTL mapping for the YRI was conducted using genotype data obtained from RNA-seq reads (i.e., the same pipeline used for the baboons), we identified 290 genes with eQTL (41.4% of those identified using independently collected genotype data).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of eQTL detected in YRI using the RNA-seq pipeline.

claim: The RNA-seq-based pipeline reduces the number of genes with detectable eQTL by 50–60% compared to using genotyping array data.
source: The RNA-seq-based pipeline therefore reduces the number of genes with detectable eQTL by 50–60%, suggesting that if genotyping array data had been available for the baboons, we might have identified eQTL for ∼3500–4000 genes
evidence: The manuscript estimates the reduction in eQTL detection based on comparison with array-based genotyping.

claim: The minor allele frequency spectrum of variants in the baboon data set included proportionally more intermediate frequency variants and proportionally fewer low frequency variants than in the human data set.
source: We observed that the minor allele frequency (MAF) spectrum of variants called in the baboon data set included proportionally more intermediate frequency variants and proportionally fewer low frequency variants than in the human data set
evidence: The manuscript reports differences in MAF distributions between baboon and human datasets.

claim: The power to identify an eQTL of effect size equal to the mean estimated beta in baboons (0.96) is increased in the Amboseli baboons by approximately 1.34-fold as a function of differences in the MAF spectrum alone.
source: Based on these differences, we estimate that the power to identify an eQTL of effect size equal to the mean estimated beta in baboons (0.96), is increased in the Amboseli baboons by approximately 1.34-fold (Figure 2A, solid purple line vs solid orange line) as a function of differences in the MAF spectrum alone.
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation-based estimates of power differences due to MAF spectrum.

claim: In baboons, an average of 45.4 (±57.0 s.d.) genetic variants were tested for each gene, whereas in YRI an average of 20.3 (±21.4 s.d.) testable variants per gene were available.
source: Indeed, in baboons we tested an average of 45.4 (±57.0 s.d.) genetic variants for each gene, whereas applying the same pipeline in YRI yielded an average of 20.3 (±21.4 s.d.) testable variants per gene.
evidence: The manuscript reports the average number of testable variants per gene in both datasets.

claim: SNP density and LD effects increase power to detect eQTL by 1.21-fold and 1.43-fold, respectively, when causal SNPs are not typed.
source: Specifically, for an eQTL that explains 28% of the variance in gene expression levels (the mean PVE detected in baboons for genes with significant eQTL), we estimate that SNP density and LD effects increase power by 1.21-fold (Figure 2B, purple dashed line vs pink dashed line) and 1.43-fold (Figure 2B, pink dashed line vs orange dashed line), respectively, when causal SNPs are not typed.
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation-based estimates of power contributions from SNP density and LD.

claim: The MAF spectrum, genetic diversity, and LD patterns increase the number of genes with detectable eQTL in baboons vs the YRI by 2.35-fold overall.
source: Together, our simulations suggest that the MAF spectrum, genetic diversity, and LD patterns increase the number of genes with detectable eQTL in baboons vs the YRI by 2.35-fold overall (1.34× from the MAF, 1.21× from SNP density effects, and 1.43× from LD effects).
evidence: The manuscript reports combined estimates from simulations of factors affecting eQTL detection power.

claim: Genes harboring eQTL in baboons were more likely to have detectable eQTL in the YRI (hypergeometric test, p = 2.39 × 10−8).
source: Interestingly, we found that genes harboring eQTL in baboons were also more likely to have detectable eQTL in the YRI (hypergeometric test, p = 2.39 × 10−8)
evidence: The manuscript reports a statistical test showing overlap of eQTL genes between species.

claim: Genes with eQTL in baboons, YRI, or both are more likely to be conserved across long stretches of evolutionary time based on mean phyloP scores (n = 7268; p < 10−53).
source: (A) Genes that harbor detectable eQTL in baboons, the YRI, or both are more likely to be conserved across long stretches of evolutionary time, based on mean phyloP scores in a 46-way primate genome comparison (n = 7268; p < 10−53).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of conservation scores for genes with eQTL, referencing Figure 3A.

claim: Genes with eQTL in both species were less likely to have orthologues in deeply diverged species based on Homologene annotations (β = −0.036, p = 1.78 × 10−8).
source: However, genes with eQTL in both species were also less likely to have orthologues in deeply diverged species, based on conservation in Homologene (β = −0.036, p = 1.78 × 10−8; Figure 3B).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis of Homologene conservation for genes with eQTL.

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between eQTL effect size and minor allele frequency in baboons (r = −0.723, p < 10−280).
source: Consistent with this idea, plotting eQTL effect size vs MAF in the baboons results in a very strong, highly significant negative correlation (r = −0.723, p < 10−280; Figure 3C)
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation statistics between eQTL effect size and MAF.

claim: When simulating sets of eQTL with constant small effect sizes (β = 0.75), the relationship between estimated effect size and MAF among detected eQTL almost perfectly recapitulated the observed negative correlation.
source: Indeed, when we simulated sets of eQTL with constant small effect sizes (β = 0.75, close to the mean effect size detected for SNPs with MAF ≥0.4), we found that the relationship between estimated effect size and MAF among detected eQTL almost perfectly recapitulated the observed negative correlation.
evidence: The manuscript reports simulation results showing winner's curse effects can explain the observed correlation.

claim: The median additive genetic proportion of variance explained (PVE) for gene expression levels in baboons was 28.4%.
source: Specifically, the median additive genetic PVE was 28.4%, similar to, or slightly greater than, estimates from human populations
evidence: The manuscript reports the median genetic PVE estimate from the analysis.

claim: The median PVE explained by age was 1.89% and by sex was 0.82%.
source: In contrast to the substantial genetic effects we detected, the median PVE explained by age and sex were 1.89% and 0.82%, respectively (Figure 4—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: The manuscript reports median PVE estimates for demographic variables.

claim: The distribution of PVE explained by age was significantly greater than expected by chance (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test: p < 10−11).
source: The distribution of PVE explained by age was significantly greater than expected by chance (Kolmogorov–Smirnov test on binned PVEs, in comparison to permuted data: p < 10−11)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing observed to permuted data.

claim: The distribution of PVE explained by sex was not significantly greater than expected by chance (p = 0.100).
source: whereas that explained by sex was not (p = 0.100)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results for sex effects on gene expression.

claim: Maternal social connectedness to males explained more variance in gene expression levels than expected by chance (p = 4.19 × 10−3), with a median PVE of 1.9%.
source: Of the early environmental variables we investigated, only maternal social connectedness to males explained more variance in gene expression levels than expected by chance (p = 4.19 × 10−3), with a median PVE of 1.9%.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results and PVE estimates for environmental variables.

claim: Primate evolution has been argued to result, in part, from changes in how genes are regulated.
source: Primate evolution has been argued to result, in part, from changes in how genes are regulated.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established argument in the field.

claim: Gene regulatory variation has been shown to make fundamental contributions to phenotypic variation in every species examined to date.
source: Gene regulatory variation has been shown to make fundamental contributions to phenotypic variation in every species examined to date.
evidence: The manuscript states this as established scientific knowledge.

claim: Variation in gene expression levels has been linked to fitness-related morphological, physiological, and behavioral variation in both lab settings and natural populations.
source: Variation in gene expression levels has been linked to fitness-related morphological, physiological, and behavioral variation in both lab settings and natural populations (e.g., Abzhanov et al., 2004; Hammock and Young, 2005; Tishkoff et al., 2006; Chan et al., 2010; reviewed in Wray, 2007)
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies supporting this claim.

claim: Patterns of gene expression are often associated with signatures of natural selection.
source: In addition, patterns of gene expression are often associated with signatures of natural selection (Rifkin et al., 2003; Denver et al., 2005; Gilad et al., 2006a; Blekhman et al., 2008)
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing associations between gene expression and selection signatures.

claim: Gene expression patterns associated with neurological development appear to have experienced an accelerated rate of change in primates relative to other mammals.
source: For example, gene expression patterns associated with neurological development appear to have experienced an accelerated rate of change in primates relative to other mammals, with axonogenesis-related and cell adhesion-related genes accelerated specifically in the human lineage (Brawand et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing accelerated evolution of neurological gene expression in primates.

claim: Differentially expressed genes in human liver are enriched for metabolic function.
source: Similarly, differentially expressed genes in human liver are enriched for metabolic function (Blekhman et al., 2008)
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing enrichment of metabolic genes in human liver.

claim: No estimates of the heritability of gene expression traits are available for natural nonhuman primate populations, even for populations that have been intensively studied for many decades.
source: No estimates of the heritability of gene expression traits are available, even for populations that have been intensively studied for many decades.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of such data as a gap in the literature.

claim: Humans exhibit low levels of neutral genetic diversity and a low long-term effective population size compared to other primates.
source: However, increasing evidence indicates that humans are demographically unusual: compared to other primates, humans exhibit low levels of neutral genetic diversity and a low long-term effective population size (Chen and Li, 2001; Hernandez et al., 2007; Perry et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing demographic differences between humans and other primates.

claim: Humans are distinguished from other primates by recent explosive population growth.
source: Further, humans are distinguished from other primates by recent explosive population growth (Keinan and Clark, 2012; Tennessen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies documenting human population expansion.

claim: The Amboseli baboon population has experienced recent admixture between yellow baboons and anubis baboons.
source: In particular, the population has experienced recent admixture between yellow baboons, the dominant taxon, and closely related anubis baboons (P. anubis) (Alberts and Altmann, 2001; Tung et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript cites studies documenting admixture in the Amboseli population.

claim: The Amboseli baboon population has been studied continuously for 43 years.
source: 43 years of prior research on this population have established it as an important model for human social behavior, health, and aging (Alberts and Altmann, 2012)
evidence: The manuscript states the duration of research on this population.

claim: Blood samples were collected from 63 individually recognized adult baboons (26 females and 37 males) from the Amboseli population.
source: Study subjects were 63 individually recognized adult members (26 females and 37 males) of the Amboseli baboon population.
evidence: The manuscript describes the sample composition.

claim: Gene expression levels were estimated for 10,409 genes expressed in whole blood.
source: After subsequent read processing and normalization steps ('Materials and methods', Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 2), we considered variation in gene expression levels for 10,409 genes expressed in whole blood
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of genes analyzed for gene expression.

claim: The final SNP call set contained 64,432 single nucleotide polymorphisms after quality control filtering.
source: These steps resulted in a set of 64,432 single nucleotide polymorphisms carried forward into downstream analysis (30,938 for the YRI).
evidence: The manuscript reports the number of SNPs retained after filtering.

claim: Of the 30,938 sites identified from RNA-seq data in YRI that passed all filters, only 3.1% (967) did not have an assigned rsID in dbSNP release 138.
source: Of the 30,938 sites that we identified from the RNA-seq data and that passed all of our filters, only 3.1% (967) did not have an assigned rsID in dbSNP release 138.
evidence: The manuscript reports validation of variant discovery using dbSNP.

claim: Regressing out the first 10 principal components of gene expression data greatly improves the ability to detect eQTL.
source: Gene expression values were first corrected for hidden factors that could act as sources of global structure (e.g., batch effects or ancestry- or environment-related trans effects) by regressing out the first 10 principal components of the gene expression data. Consistent with previous results (e.g., Pickrell et al., 2010a), this procedure greatly improves our ability to detect eQTL (Figure 1—figure supplement 12).
evidence: The manuscript describes a methodological improvement and cites supporting evidence.

claim: Genes involved in basic cellular metabolic processes were under-enriched among the set of genes with eQTL in both species.
source: Consistent with this idea, genes involved in basic cellular metabolic processes were under-enriched among the set of genes with eQTL in both species, and enriched among the set of genes for which no eQTL were detected in either species (Supplementary file 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis results for genes with eQTL.

claim: The set of genes with eQTL in either or both species were enriched for loci involved in antigen processing, catalytic activity, and interaction with the extracellular environment.
source: The set of genes with eQTL in either or both species, on the other hand, were enriched for loci involved in antigen processing, catalytic activity, and interaction with the extracellular environment (e.g., receptors, membrane-associated proteins).
evidence: The manuscript reports enrichment analysis results for genes with eQTL.

claim: Large sex effects on gene expression tended to be constrained to a small set of genes on the X chromosome.
source: large sex effects tended to be constrained to a small set of genes on the X chromosome (Figure 4—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The manuscript reports the chromosomal distribution of sex effects on gene expression.

claim: Social connectedness to males and social connectedness to females are both known predictors of longevity in the Amboseli baboons, with largely independent effects.
source: Notably, while social connectedness to males (i.e., heterosexual bonds) and social connectedness to females (i.e., same-sex bonds) are both known predictors of longevity in the Amboseli baboons, previous analyses suggest that their effects are largely independent (Archie et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing independent effects of different types of social bonds on longevity.

claim: Demographic history does not impact overall trait heritability.
source: Interestingly, demographic history does not impact overall trait heritability (Lohmueller, 2014; Simons et al., 2014), perhaps explaining why we estimated mean additive genetic PVEs for gene expression levels in baboons that are similar to those estimated for humans.
evidence: The manuscript cites studies showing demographic history does not affect heritability.

claim: Demographic history can influence the power to detect individual genetic contributions to phenotypic variation.
source: However, demographic history can influence the power to detect individual genetic contributions to phenotypic variation.
evidence: The manuscript states this as an established principle.

claim: Large-scale population expansion of the type that occurred in human history appears to reduce power to identify genotype-phenotype correlations for fitness-related traits.
source: Large-scale population expansion of the type that occurred in human history appears to reduce power to identify genotype-phenotype correlations for fitness-related traits (Lohmueller, 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites a study showing effects of population expansion on mapping power.

claim: This study represents the first profile of genome-wide gene expression levels in a wild primate population.
source: Finally, our data—the first profile of genome-wide gene expression levels in a wild primate population—serve as a useful proof of principle of the ability to concurrently generate genome-wide gene expression phenotype and genotype data
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this is the first such study.

claim: The study establishes the feasibility of eQTL mapping using RNA-seq data alone.
source: Further, they establish the feasibility of eQTL mapping using RNA-seq data alone, and represent an important step towards understanding the genetic architecture of gene expression in primates.
evidence: The manuscript states this as a key finding from the study.

claim: Genes vary in their tolerance of genetic perturbation, and this property may be conserved across species.
source: Our results suggest that genes vary in their tolerance of genetic perturbation, and that this property may be conserved across species.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the cross-species eQTL overlap analysis.

claim: The correlation between eQTL effect size and minor allele frequency in baboons does not provide strong support for widespread negative selection on gene expression phenotypes within species.
source: Hence, the correlation between estimated eQTL effect size and MAF in the baboons does not provide strong support for widespread negative selection on gene expression phenotypes within species.
evidence: The manuscript concludes this based on simulation results showing winner's curse effects.

claim: Genetic effects on gene expression levels tended to be far more pervasive than demographic and environmental effects.
source: Overall, we found that genetic effects on gene expression levels tended to be far more pervasive than demographic and environmental effects.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the relative contributions of different factors to gene expression variation.

claim: Early environmental effects on gene expression levels appear to persist across the life course in at least some cases.
source: However, in at least some cases, we find evidence that early environmental effects on gene expression levels appear to persist across the life course, as has previously been demonstrated in laboratory settings and in response to severe early adversity in humans (e.g., Weaver et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2009; Cole et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the analysis of maternal social connectedness effects and cites supporting studies.

claim: eQTL are least likely to be detected for strongly conserved loci and most likely to be detected for lineage-specific, rapidly evolving genes.
source: Thus, sequence-level conservation scores and depth of homology across species combine to suggest that eQTL—or at least those with relatively large effect sizes—are least likely to be detected for strongly conserved loci, and most likely to be detected for lineage-specific, rapidly evolving genes.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from conservation and Homologene analyses.

claim: Controlling for local structure when testing for eQTL still results in a large excess of eQTL detected in the baboon data set (∼7× higher than in YRI).
source: However, this explanation seems unlikely because evidence for ASE does not extend further from tested genes in baboons compared to YRI (Figure 1—figure supplement 10), and because adding controls for local (chromosome-specific) structure when testing for eQTL still results in a large excess of eQTL detected in the baboon data set (∼7× fold higher than in YRI: 'Materials and methods' and Figure 1—figure supplement 11)
evidence: The manuscript reports results from analysis controlling for local structure.

claim: Adding a control for local structure modestly reduced the number of eQTL discoveries in the baboon data set from 1787 to 1583 (an 11.4% difference).
source: We found that this approach modestly reduced the number of eQTL discoveries in the baboon data set (n = 1583 from n = 1787, an 11.4% difference).
evidence: The manuscript reports the effect of controlling for local structure on eQTL detection.

claim: The locations of eQTL were very similar under models with and without local structure controls (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p = 0.577).
source: However, the locations of eQTL were very similar under both models (Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, p = 0.577; Figure 1—figure supplement 11).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical comparison of eQTL locations under different models.

claim: Whole blood from baboons and lymphoblastoid cell lines from YRI exhibit highly correlated but not identical patterns of overall gene expression (Spearman's rho = 0.645, p < 1 × 10−16).
source: Comparisons that use matched sample types will be particularly informative: our study compared eQTL detection in whole blood (from the baboons) with eQTL from lymphoblastoid cell lines (YRI), which exhibit highly correlated, but not identical, patterns of overall gene expression (Spearman's rho = 0.645, p < 1 × 10−16)
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation between gene expression patterns in different sample types.

claim: Reference allele homozygotes tend to have higher coverage than alternate allele homozygotes (K-S test: p < 2.2 × 10−16 for all SNPs; p = 3.9 × 10−5 for eQTL SNPs).
source: Reference allele homozygotes tend to have higher coverage, on average, than alternate allele homozygotes (K-S test: p < 2.2 × 10−16 for all SNPs; p = 3.9 × 10−5 for eQTL SNPs)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical tests of coverage differences by genotype class.

claim: The magnitude of reference allele mapping bias is smaller for eQTL SNPs than for all SNPs (K-S D = 0.167 for all SNPs; K-S D = 0.084 for eQTL SNPs).
source: however the effect is actually smaller for eQTL SNPs than for all SNPs (K-S D = 0.167 for all SNPs; K-S D = 0.084 for eQTL SNPs)
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of mapping bias between SNP sets.

claim: 47% of eQTL betas are negative, whereas 53% are positive.
source: Our data are not consistent with such a pattern: 47% of eQTL betas are negative, whereas 53% are positive.
evidence: The manuscript reports the distribution of eQTL effect directions.

claim: There is a modest excess of eQTL for which the major allele was associated with lower gene expression levels (56%, binomial test p = 1.15 × 10−7).
source: We observed a modest excess of eQTL for which the major allele was associated with lower gene expression levels (56%, binomial test p = 1.15 × 10−7).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test of directional bias in eQTL effects.

claim: The directional bias in eQTL effects did not differ depending on whether the major allele was the reference allele or the alternate allele (Fisher's Exact Test, p = 0.28).
source: This bias did not differ depending on whether the major allele was the reference allele or the alternate allele (Fisher's Exact Test, p = 0.28)
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test ruling out reference allele mapping bias as explanation.

claim: The directional bias in eQTL effects appears to be primarily driven by SNPs with low minor allele frequencies (proportion of negative betas for the lowest quartile of MAFs = 62.8%, p = 7.49 × 10−8; highest quartile of MAFs = 48.6%, p = 0.602).
source: Instead, it appears to be primarily driven by SNPs with low minor allele frequencies (proportion of negative betas for the lowest quartile of MAFs = 62.8%, p = 7.49 × 10−8; highest quartile of MAFs = 48.6%, p = 0.602).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of directional bias by MAF quartile.

claim: Effect size magnitude is highly correlated across RNA-seq and conventional pipelines when eQTL are discovered in both pipelines (r = 0.874, p < 10−57).
source: Further, effect size magnitude is highly correlated across pipelines when eQTL are discovered in both pipelines (r = 0.874, p < 10−57).
evidence: The manuscript reports correlation of effect sizes between different genotyping methods.

claim: eQTL discovered only in the RNA-seq pipeline tended to be high on the ranked list of eQTL evidence in the conventional pipeline as well (median rank of 1395, where the top 700 were significant and 10,615 genes were tested).
source: When eQTL were discovered only in the RNA-seq pipeline (n = 104), they tended to be high on the ranked list of eQTL evidence in the conventional pipeline as well (median rank of 1395, where the top 700 were significant and 10,615 genes were tested)
evidence: The manuscript reports comparison of eQTL rankings between pipelines.
